title: Quickstart
text:
Choose Your Model


What do you want to do?
I need protein sequence embeddings or representations → Use ESMC or ESM2 (Embeddings Tutorial)
I want to design new proteins or generate sequences → Use ESM3 (Design Tutorial)
I need to predict protein 3D structure

Single chain? → Use ESMFold or ESMFold2 (Structure Tutorial)
Complex (antibody-antigen, multimer)? → Use ESMFold2 (Complex Prediction Tutorial)
Need maximum speed? → Use ESMFold2-Fast (Performance Guide)

I’m working with legacy code → Use ESM2 (Migration Guide)
I want to fine-tune a model → Use ESMC (Fine-tuning Guide)

title: Quickstart
text:
Installation

Quick Start
# Install the ESM package
pip install esm

# Or from GitHub for latest version
pip install git+https://github.com/Biohub/esm.git@main
Requirements
Python 3.10+ PyTorch 2.0+ CUDA 11.8+ (for GPU acceleration)
For detailed setup instructions, see the Installation Guide.
Next Steps Once you’ve chosen your model:
Read the Full Decision Tree for detailed guidance Check the Model Comparison for specs Follow a Tutorial to learn by doing Browse Use Cases to see real examples
Contribute to This Page Help us improve this guide! 🔗 Suggest improvements{.btn .btn-secondary}

title: Decision Tree
text:
Use this interactive guide to find the right ESM model for your project.






→ Go to Section 2A

I’m doing research and want the best representations → Use ESMC (latest, best quality, metagenomic training) - Model Card - Tutorial: Getting Embeddings - GitHub
I have existing ESM2 code and want to upgrade → Use ESMC (drop-in replacement, but see migration guide) - Migration Guide - Comparison Table
I’m using legacy code tied to ESM2 → Stay with ESM2 (for now) - ESM2 Docs - Plan migration to ESMC when ready
I want to fine-tune on my own data → Use ESMC - Fine-tuning Tutorial - Larger models (6B) work best, but 300M is faster for experiments
I need this to be very fast → Use ESMC-300M - Smallest model, still high quality - Much faster inference than larger models







De novo proteins (completely new sequences) → Use ESM3 - Model Card - Design Tutorial - Paper
Protein binders (antibodies, miniproteins) → Use ESM3 with ESMFold2 - Generate sequences with ESM3 - Validate structures with ESMFold2 - Binder Design Example
Enzyme variants (improving existing proteins) → Use ESMC + ESMFold2 - Score mutations with ESMC embeddings - Validate with structure prediction - Directed Evolution Example







Single protein chain (monomers) → Use ESMFold2-Fast - Fastest option - Excellent accuracy - Tutorial
Protein complexes (antibody-antigen, PPIs, multimers) → Use ESMFold2 - State-of-the-art accuracy - Handles up to 768 residues (all chains combined) - Complex Prediction Tutorial
Large complexes (>768 residues) → Use ESMFold2-Fast on individual chains, then dock manually - Or use Docking Tools - Future versions may support longer sequences
I need maximum accuracy → Use ESMFold2 with MSA - Request on Biohub - 3-5% better accuracy with multiple sequence alignment
I need to screen thousands of structures quickly → Use ESMFold2-Fast - 1.3x faster than ESMFold2 - Minimal accuracy trade-off







Predict effects of all possible mutations (variant effect prediction) → Use ESMC with log-likelihood ratios - Mutation Scoring Tutorial - Variant Prediction Example
Find stabilizing mutations for protein engineering → Use ESMC + ESMFold2 - Score with ESMC - Validate stability with structure - Stability Engineering Example
Understand disease-causing mutations → Use ESMC - Disease Prediction Tutorial - Compare wild-type vs. mutant log-likelihood
Protein function prediction → Use ESMC - Function information in layer 50-60 - Function Prediction Example

title: Contributing to Awesome ESM
text:
We’re excited to have you contribute! This resource is built by and for the ESM community.




Found a great paper using ESM? Share it!
Open an issue with: - Title - Link to paper - Brief summary (2-3 sentences) - Which ESM model(s) were used - Your name/affiliation



Is something confusing? Help us improve documentation.
Open an issue with: - Your question (in user language) - Suggested answer - Code example (if applicable)



Found a typo, broken link, or outdated info?
Open an issue and let us know what needs fixing.



Want to see a tutorial on a specific topic?
Open an issue to request one.
To contribute a tutorial: - Check that it’s not already listed - Open a pull request with the tutorial notebook/script - Link to the tutorial from the Tutorials page






git clone https://github.com/Biohub/awesome-esm.git

quarto preview
Making Changes
Create a new branch: git checkout -b my-contribution Make your changes Preview locally: quarto preview Commit: git commit -am “Add: description of change” Push: git push origin my-contribution Open a pull request

text:
Research focused on developing new ESM models, improving architectures, and advancing protein language modeling.
Papers in this section describe the models themselves and methodological advances that enable better representations of protein biology.

title: Get Involved
text:
Awesome ESM is built by and for the community. We welcome contributions of all kinds!



By contributing, you help: - Researchers discover new papers and use cases - Developers find code examples and best practices - Everyone build better understanding of protein language models






Found a great paper using ESM models? Help us build our collection!
What to include: - Paper title and link - Brief summary (2-3 sentences) - Which ESM model(s) were used - How ESM was used (technique/application) - Your name and affiliation
📝 Add a paper




Have you built something interesting with ESM? Tell us about it!
What to include: - Title of your project/analysis - Brief description - ESM model(s) used - Key results or findings - Code/notebooks if you’d like to share - Your contact info
💡 Share a use case




Is something confusing? Help us improve documentation!
What to include: - Your question (in plain language) - Suggested answer - Code example (if applicable) - Links to relevant resources
❓ Suggest FAQ entry




Want to see a tutorial on a specific topic?
To request: 📺 Request a tutorial
To contribute: - Create a Jupyter notebook or script - Include clear documentation - Test your code thoroughly - Submit a pull request
📤 Contribute a tutorial




Found a typo, broken link, or error?
🐛 Report an issue




Want to contribute code, design, or documentation improvements?
Get started: 1. Fork the repository 2. Create a branch for your changes 3. Submit a pull request
See CONTRIBUTING.md for detailed guidelines.
💻 View guidelines








Be kind and welcoming to all contributors
Assume good intent
Respect others’ perspectives





Link to original sources
Include proper citations
Verify information before submitting





Contributions should relate to ESM models or protein language models
No spam or promotional content
Focus on quality over quantity




We review contributions to ensure they’re: - ✅ Relevant to ESM - ✅ Accurate and well-sourced - ✅ Not spam or duplicates
We don’t review for scientific merit—just quality and relevance.





Contributors are recognized in: - Pull request comments (GitHub) - Paper table contributor column - Monthly contributor highlights (coming soon)

title: FAQ
text:
A: Use ESMC for new projects. It’s the latest, trained on 2.8B diverse metagenomic sequences, and provides higher-quality representations than ESM2.
If you have existing ESM2 code, ESMC is a drop-in replacement with similar API. See our Decision Tree for detailed guidance.
Related: Model Comparison | Getting Started




A: - ESMC: Newer (2025), trained on 2.8B metagenomic + UniRef sequences, better quality, log-linear scaling - ESM2: Older (2023), trained on 50M UniRef sequences, still good for many tasks
For new projects, use ESMC. ESM2 is good for legacy workflows.
Related: Model Comparison | Migration Guide




A: - ESMFold2: State-of-the-art accuracy (best for publications, critical applications) - ESMFold2-Fast: 1.3x faster with minimal accuracy loss (best for screening, high-throughput)
Minimal difference on simple single-chain predictions. Complex predictions (antibody-antigen) benefit more from ESMFold2.
Related: Model Comparison | Decision Tree




A: No. ESM3 is designed for protein design and generation. For structure prediction alone, use ESMFold2. For embeddings, use ESMC.
ESM3 is best when you need to generate new sequences or make conditional predictions.
Related: Decision Tree | Use Cases









A:
pip install esm
Or for the latest development version:
pip install git+https://github.com/Biohub/esm.git@main
Requirements: - Python 3.10+ - PyTorch 2.0+ - CUDA 11.8+ (for GPU acceleration)
Related: Getting Started | Tutorials




A: No. You can download ESMC and ESMFold2 from HuggingFace and run them locally without authentication.
You only need an API key if you’re using the Biohub web platform.
Links: HuggingFace Models | Biohub API




A: - Embeddings (ESMC): Can run on CPU, but GPU (4GB VRAM) much faster - Structure Prediction (ESMFold2): GPU recommended (16GB+ VRAM for large complexes) - Design: Depends on inference-time search budget
For production use, 24GB VRAM GPU recommended.
Related: Model Comparison









A: See our Embeddings Tutorial.
Quick code:
import esm

model = esm.pretrained.esmfold_v1()
sequences = ["MKFLK...", "MKVLA..."]
embeddings = model(sequences)
Related: Tutorial | Decision Tree




A: - Single chain (1024 aa): ~15 seconds (ESMFold2), ~10 seconds (ESMFold2-Fast) on H100 GPU - Complex (2x 300 aa): ~30 seconds - CPU: 10-100x slower
Time scales roughly linearly with sequence length.
Related: Model Comparison | Performance Benchmarks




A: ESMFold2 has a 2048 token limit total (all chains combined).
Options: 1. Predict individual chains separately, then dock 2. Use overlapping window approach 3. Request support in Biohub for longer sequences
Related: Known Limitations | Decision Tree




A: Use log-likelihood ratio approach:
# Get likelihood for wild-type and mutant
wt_likelihood = model(sequence)["logits"][position, wt_aa]
mut_likelihood = model(mutant_seq)["logits"][position, mut_aa]

# Compute log-likelihood ratio
score = mut_likelihood - wt_likelihood
See our Mutation Scoring Tutorial.
Related: Tutorial | Use Cases









A: Yes, use ESM3. It generates novel protein sequences conditioned on structure and function properties.
See our Design Tutorial and Design Use Cases.
Related: Decision Tree | Use Cases




A: - Antibody-antigen: 50-55% DockQ ≥ 0.23 (single sequence), 55%+ with MSA - Protein-protein: 70-76% success rate - Single chains: Very high accuracy (similar to AlphaFold)
Accuracy depends on sequence quality and complexity.
Related: Model Comparison | Benchmarks




A: ESMFold2 supports small molecule ligands as SMILES strings.
See our Ligand Binding Tutorial.
Related: Tutorial | Use Cases









A: Yes. ESMC fine-tunes well with modest amounts of task-specific data.
Best practices: - Use smaller models (300M or 600M) for faster iteration - Start with a small learning rate - Use parameter-efficient methods (LoRA)
See our Fine-tuning Tutorial.
Related: Tutorial | Use Cases




A: It depends on your task: - Simple properties (e.g., solubility): 100-1000 examples - Complex properties (e.g., binding): 1000-10000 examples - Rare tasks: May need more
Start small and scale up based on performance.
Related: Fine-tuning Tutorial









A: - ESMC, ESM3, ESMFold2: MIT License (open source) - ESM2: MIT License - Check official repository for latest: github.com/Biohub/esm
See LICENSE for details.




A: Yes. ESM models are released under MIT License, which permits commercial use.
See the license file for full terms.









A: - GitHub Issues: Report bugs or ask questions - GitHub Discussions: Join the community discussion - Slack: Join our community - Biohub: Contact support

See CONTRIBUTING.md.

A: - Embeddings (ESMC): Can run on CPU, but GPU (4GB VRAM) much faster - Structure Prediction (ESMFold2): GPU recommended (16GB+ VRAM for large complexes) - Design: Depends on inference-time search budget
For production use, 24GB VRAM GPU recommended.
Related: Model Comparison

A: - Single chain (1024 aa): ~15 seconds (ESMFold2), ~10 seconds (ESMFold2-Fast) on H100 GPU - Complex (2x 300 aa): ~30 seconds - CPU: 10-100x slower
Time scales roughly linearly with sequence length.
Related: Model Comparison | Performance Benchmarks




A: ESMFold2 has a 2048 token limit total (all chains combined).
Options: 1. Predict individual chains separately, then dock 2. Use overlapping window approach 3. Request support in Biohub for longer sequences
Related: Known Limitations | Decision Tree




A: Use log-likelihood ratio approach:
# Get likelihood for wild-type and mutant
wt_likelihood = model(sequence)["logits"][position, wt_aa]
mut_likelihood = model(mutant_seq)["logits"][position, mut_aa]

# Compute log-likelihood ratio
score = mut_likelihood - wt_likelihood
See our Mutation Scoring Tutorial.

title: Awesome ESM
text:
What is Awesome ESM?
This resource is a community-driven hub for the ESM family of protein language models:

ESM-C (ESMC) - The latest sequence representation model
ESM3 - Multimodal protein design and prediction
ESM2 - High-performance sequence representations
ESMFold - Structure prediction from sequence alone
ESMFold2 - State-of-the-art biomolecular complex prediction

Whether you’re predicting protein structures, designing new binders, discovering novel enzymes, or analyzing protein properties, you’ll find resources, examples, and community insights here.

title: Model Comparison
text:
Status: Latest (2025)
Parameters: 300M, 600M, 6B
Training Data: 2.8B metagenomic sequences
Best For: - Sequence embeddings and representations - Function prediction - Fine-tuning for custom tasks - Mutation scoring - Zero-shot variant effect prediction
Key Features: - Trained on metagenomic data (more diverse) - Log-linear scaling with compute - Better representations than ESM2 - Supported via Biohub API
Access: Biohub | HuggingFace | GitHub




Status: Previous generation (2023)
Parameters: 8M - 15B
Training Data: 50M UniProt sequences
Best For: - Legacy workflows - Projects using existing ESM2 code - When you have established pipelines
Key Features: - Well-established - Large community resources - Lots of published examples
Migration Note: ESMC is a drop-in replacement but with some API differences. See Migration Guide.
Access: HuggingFace | GitHub







Status: Latest (2025)
Architecture: Stable recurrent folding layers
Modes: Single sequence or MSA-augmented
Best For: - Protein complex prediction - Antibody-antigen interactions - Protein-protein interactions - Multi-chain systems - When accuracy is critical
Key Features: - State-of-the-art accuracy - Inference-time scaling - Faster than AlphaFold3 - Supports ligand binding
Input Limits: - Single sequence: up to 768 residues - Complex mode: sum of chains ≤ 768 residues
Performance: - Antibody-antigen: 50-55% DockQ pass rate - Protein-protein: 70-76% pass rate - Protein-ligand: 63-66% pass rate
Access: Biohub | Tutorials




Status: Latest (2025)
Architecture: Simplified, optimized for speed
Best For: - High-throughput structure prediction - Screening large sequence sets - When speed matters more than maximum accuracy - Monomer or simple predictions
Key Features: - 50% fewer layers than ESMFold2 - No MSA requirement - 1.3x faster than ESMFold2 - Minimal accuracy trade-off
Performance: - Antibody-antigen: 50% DockQ pass rate - Protein-protein: 68% pass rate - Protein-ligand: 63% pass rate
Access: Biohub | Tutorials




Status: First generation (2022)
Best For: - Legacy workflows - When ESMFold2 is unavailable
Note: Use ESMFold2 instead—it’s faster and more accurate.
Access: GitHub







Status: Latest (2025)
Modalities: Sequence, structure, function
Best For: - De novo protein design - Sequence generation - Conditional structure prediction - Protein engineering
Key Features: - Multimodal (seq + structure + function) - Can generate from partial inputs - Great for design workflows
Access: Biohub | Paper | Tutorials
